details:
**Pericles and the Funeral Oration**
Pericles was the leading statesman of Athens during its fifth-century BCE Golden Age, often called its "first citizen." His Funeral Oration for the first dead of the Peloponnesian War, recorded by Thucydides, praises Athenian democracy and contains lines such as "famous men have the whole earth as their memorial." He died in the plague of 429 BCE.

**Peloponnesian War and the Battle of Aegospotami**
The war (431–404 BCE) between Athens and Sparta. Thucydides, an Athenian general, wrote that its real cause was the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta; immediate triggers included disputes over Corcyra and Potidaea and the Megarian Decree's economic sanctions on Megara. Athens lost after the Spartan admiral Lysander destroyed its fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE.

**Thirty Tyrants**
The pro-Spartan oligarchy installed by Lysander after Athens surrendered in 404 BCE. Led by Critias, with Theramenes as a more moderate member, it limited full rights to a list of 3,000 citizens and executed many opponents. The exiled democrat Thrasybulus seized the hill fort of Phyle, defeated them, and Critias was killed, which restored the democracy in 403 BCE.

**Ostracism**
The Athenian procedure in which citizens scratched the name of a man they wanted exiled onto pottery shards called ostraka. The "winner" was banished for ten years without losing his property. It is usually credited to Cleisthenes; Hipparchus, son of Charmus, was the first man ostracized, and Themistocles was later ostracized as well.

**Cleisthenes**
The Alcmaeonid reformer of around 508 BCE, often called the father of Athenian democracy. He reorganized citizens into ten tribes made of local units called demes and expanded the Boule from 400 to 500 members (50 per tribe). He overcame his rival Isagoras, who was backed by Sparta.

**Boule (Council of 500)**
The council of 500 citizens, 50 chosen by lot from each of the ten tribes, that prepared business for the Ekklesia, the assembly of all adult male citizens. Most Athenian offices were filled by sortition (random lot), except the elected generals (strategoi).

**Draco**
The lawgiver who wrote Athens' first written law code around 621 BCE. It was so harsh, with death as the penalty even for stealing cabbages, that "draconian" now means excessively severe.

**Solon**
The early-sixth-century BCE archon who repealed most of Draco's laws (except those on homicide), cancelled debts and ended debt slavery. He divided citizens into four property classes, the lowest being the thetes; his laws were displayed on rotating wooden tablets called axones, and he then left Athens for ten years.

**Delian League**
The alliance of Greek city-states formed in 478 BCE against Persia and named for its original treasury on the island of Delos. Athens, with Cimon as an early commander, turned it into an empire; it moved the treasury to Athens and used the tribute (phoros) to pay for the Parthenon.

**Parthenon and the Acropolis**
The temple to Athena Parthenos, the city's patron goddess, built on the Acropolis under Pericles. Phidias made its great statue of Athena, and many of its sculptures, the Elgin Marbles, were removed by Lord Elgin and are now in the British Museum.

**Sicilian Expedition and Alcibiades**
The disastrous Athenian invasion of Syracuse (415–413 BCE). Its leader Alcibiades was accused of mutilating the hermai (busts of Hermes) just before it sailed, was recalled for trial, and defected to Sparta. The Spartan general Gylippus helped Syracuse destroy the Athenian force.

**Plague of Athens**
The epidemic that struck Athens in 430 BCE, entering through the crowded port of Piraeus while the population sheltered behind the city walls. It killed a large share of the population, including Pericles; its cause is unknown, with typhus and typhoid among the suggestions.

**Themistocles, Salamis and the Long Walls**
Themistocles built up Athens' fleet of triremes, which won the naval Battle of Salamis against Persia in 480 BCE, and he fortified the port of Piraeus. The Long Walls later linked Athens to Piraeus and Phalerum so the city could be supplied by sea even during a siege. Themistocles himself was eventually ostracized.

**Aspasia**
The Milesian woman who was Pericles' companion and a metic (resident foreigner) in Athens. Comic poets accused her of immorality and blamed her for Athens' war with Samos, and Pericles defended her in court.

**Panathenaic festival and the peplos**
The great festival of Athena, during which a new woven robe (peplos) was presented to her ancient wooden statue. Selected girls helped weave the robe and served as basket-bearers in the procession; women also celebrated their own festivals such as the Thesmophoria.

**Alcmaeonid curse and the Cylonian affair**
In the seventh century BCE, the archon Megacles of the Alcmaeonid family put to death followers of Cylon, who had tried to seize power and had taken sanctuary. The family was declared cursed and exiled. Later Alcmaeonids included Cleisthenes, who helped overthrow the tyrant Hippias, and Pericles.
